a. Response/Answer: This IPC met an untimely end earlier this year, when the draft
NSM it produced failed to square the challenges of domestic vs. foreign
disinformation. The Suite pulled it down, used the planned DC instead for an
open-ended discussion of the issue, and NSC is just now preparing to reboot the
process in the next month, with a focus exclusively on disinformation abroad.
Vera Zakem and Johnny Walsh are attending; on October 27th, they met with Rob
Bershinski and Caitlin Durkovich, the new Deputy Homeland Security Advisor,
to advise on the process and brief on USAID's efforts to address MDM through
our Information Resilience Council. This Agency effort, which DA Coleman
helped us launch in September, includes periodic briefings to AAs and four
working-level groups which are assigned, respectively, to 1) assess the impact of
our programing and improve its effectiveness against disinformation; 2) help
missions and partners respond to disinformation and mitigate operational security
risk; 3) get "out front" in communicating our work; and 4) systematize our
external engagement with the tech companies, implementing partners, and the

interagency. Both Rob and Caitlin were "inspired" by our efforts, and wanted to
incorporate our insights into the rebooted IPC process.
b. The question of "who leads" foreign disinformation efforts is a relic of the
ill-fated NSM and no longer immediately relevant, though it may reemerge as the
new process takes shape. On the dollar disparity between State and USAID, it is
difficult to capture exact numbers since a variety of efforts could be considered
relevant to disinformation. As one datapoint, according to a EUR/ACE and GEC
analysis, in 2021 approximately $358 million were invested in media, civil
society and MDM efforts, with USAID and State providing 72% and 28%
respectively in E&E. USAID invests more in addressing MDM through our
programs to support independent media, address media and digital literacy,
messaging, and work by, with, and through partners to build resilience in the
information environment. State primarily invests its limited resources in analytics
through the Global Engagement Center and media literacy programming through
DRL. We would need to do additional analysis to understand the full breadth of
MDM programming at State vice at USAID for this FY.
c. The Information Resilience Council, as noted above, is currently beginning to
take stock of its programming efforts and Mission needs. Of note, USAID has a
standalone "whole-of-society" disinformation program in Georgia, which Vera
will be visiting between November 8-10th. We hope to elevate this issue through
the Summit for Democracy, potentially by adding a disinformation fund of ~$8 to
10M annually to the Presidential Initiative for Democratic Renewal (PIDR), or
possibly to seek this funding separately, so as not to dilute other PIDR programs..
2. Your comment: Updates on all this?
The team appreciates any feedback or steers on the suggested path forward on both
intra-Agency and interagency next steps. One next step we are considering is to formalize this
team and add representation from additional offices or bureaus. This task team would complete
a stock taking of all USAID assets, capabilities and gaps. As one option, we could create a
Sector Council on disinformation that DRG could co-chair with PPL to encourage coordination
across the Agency. We are also considering drafting a USAID strategy on MDM, which currently
does not exist. DAA Johnny Walsh has indicated that the first Summit for Democracy featured
little direct focus on disinformation, and it would be reasonable to look at ways to incorporate it
in deliverables this year and/or Year of Action work with partners. The team is in the early
stages of refining USAID capabilities and responses and crafting USAID's role within any
interagency coordination process, and will refine these deliverables as we develop and
strengthen the task team.
Updates on all this?

a. As noted above, we stood up the Information Resilience Council and Working
Groups focused upon Programming, USAID Security and Operations,
Communications, and External Engagement. Led by Vera Zakem, the IRC has
representation from all regional bureaus and key functional bureaus including
LPA, SEC, PPL, M, and DDI. The technical working group has had 3 meetings,
and is finalizing preliminary insights, decisions, and initial resource requests,
which it will bring forward to the senior leadership group the week after
Thanksgiving. In addition, we are piloting an innovative ad buy campaign in
Kenya and East Africa to better tell USAID's story on food security as a way to
address disinformation. The ads are going up on Facebook, You Tube, Twitter,
and messages will be disseminated via influencers on WhatsApp starting the week
of November 7th. Vera is leading this campaign from HQ and is coordinating with
the Kenya DOC. During the senior leadership meeting of the IRC after
Thanksgiving, we will examine preliminary results from this campaign, with an
eye to whether this approach is scalable for us.
3. Your question: What about the rest of USG? Need broader perspective on what is being done
by other agencies, surely.

a. As an update to the February info memo cited above, OTI currently has 24
activities addressing mis/disinformation (and hate speech) in Ethiopia. OTI has
partnered with local media outlets, media professionals, community radio stations,
youth groups, civil society organizations, traditional leaders, and other national
and regional stakeholders in this effort, and supported a biweekly social media
monitoring report to better understand the dynamics of online and conventional
media rhetoric and intercommunal violence.
b. More broadly, OTI works through local, multi-stakeholder partnerships to
mitigate the negative effects of MDM when it is defined as a critical obstacle to
peaceful and democratic transitions. OTI does not expect its programs to stop

disinformation or hate speech; however, OTI can research its effects, mitigate its
influence, and moderate its virality.
i. Interventions can include working with: 1) local media outlets on
independent fact-checking and reporting, and developing content to help
communities find commonalities around fact-counterfact debates; 2) local
civil society organizations and community leaders to raise awareness
about disinformation, hate speech, and respond to its effects; 3) local
governments to improve the quality and distribution of their strategic
communications related to public services and reforms; and 4) local
creatives to produce social impact entertainment content that reframe the
issues from immovable fact-counterfact debates to a conversation based
on deeply held values. This work is grounded in locally-driven research
and analysis on disinformation and hate speech, including the incentives,
grievances, and networks behind them.
c. The core agencies that do counter messaging are DOD and State through the GEC
and GPA. DOD has a comprehensive counter messaging program through the
U.S. Special Operations Command and Military Information Support Operations
(MISO). On October 20th, Vera Zakem attended and presented at the 11th Annual
Information Operations Conference at INDOPACOM and built relationships with
DOD to see how we can collaborate in this space. Vera is planning to visit
USSOCOM in the new year to best synergize our efforts; she and others from
DRG have also coordinated with OSD and other combatant commands on each
one's individual efforts. These efforts are also coordinated with USAID's Office
of Civil Military Cooperation.
d. State's Digital Freedom Unit with the new Bureau for Cyber and Digital Policy
has the mandate to lead the Department of State on setting foreign policy
priorities related to information integrity and content moderation issues. However,
their work is extremely nascent. The digital freedom unit is participating in the
S4D Information Integrity Cohort along with USAID and State's Global
Engagement Center (GEC). GEC is the State Department analytic and technical
lead regarding combating MDM and provides analytics organized around specific
"threat actors." This data is shared with USAID and other agencies, however it
seems to have limited usage. Our consultations with USAID field offices are
aware of GEC products but most said they are only somewhat helpful as they
either aren't focused on our countries or do not assess the impact of. In addition,
the information isn't shareable with implementing partners (and often even with
FSN staff.) GEC also provides small grants for research and local media partners
and USAID partners on some of those efforts to avoid duplication. DRL and
EUR/ ACE provide research and grants for media and digital literacy, cyber

hygiene, and other resilience building activities. However, they are more limited
in scope vis-a-vis USAID, which has programming in this space globally.
e. The intelligence community has its own capabilities here, which are best
discussed in other formats but which also have expanded over the last few years.
Johnny and others have met with the key counterparts, and are interested in
aligning (or at least deconflicting) our efforts better than AID and the IC
sometimes do. As a next step, [opaque block] has offered to help Vera and team to
put together a meeting with key IC representatives on MDM for increased
information sharing on threat assessments.
f. Broadly speaking, USAID efforts in the field are always a joint effort with State,
particularly the public affairs sections. The IR Council is currently conducting
USAID Mission consultations to better understand their context, programming
responses, and Embassy/Mission operational issues. Nearly all meetings have
either included someone from the public affairs section or have indicated
considerable USAID-State partnership in addressing MDM through
programming, information sharing, or strategic communications.
